name: Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn
aliases: hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

clinicalPearls: Immune-mediated haemolysis of fetal or neonatal red cells caused by maternal antibodies crossing the placenta and targeting fetal red cell antigens inherited from the father.
Rhesus (anti-D) disease was historically the most severe form; ABO incompatibility is now a more common but generally milder cause, and other minor blood-group antibodies can also be responsible.
Rh disease typically requires prior maternal sensitisation, so it usually spares the first pregnancy and worsens with subsequent affected pregnancies, whereas ABO disease can affect a first-born.
Severe fetal anaemia can cause hydrops fetalis with generalised oedema, effusions, hepatosplenomegaly, and heart failure.
In the newborn the dominant problem is rapidly rising unconjugated bilirubin from ongoing haemolysis, which can appear within the first day of life.
A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the infant supports immune haemolysis, along with anaemia, reticulocytosis, and a rising bilirubin.
Rh disease is largely preventable by giving anti-D immunoglobulin to at-risk Rh-negative mothers to prevent sensitisation.
Management ranges from monitoring and phototherapy for hyperbilirubinaemia to exchange transfusion for severe or rapidly rising bilirubin, and intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anaemia.
Late anaemia can develop over the following weeks as haemolysis and marrow suppression continue, so follow-up haemoglobin monitoring is important.
reference.pathophysiology: When fetal red cells carrying a paternally inherited antigen absent in the mother enter the maternal circulation, the mother may form IgG alloantibodies. These IgG antibodies cross the placenta, bind fetal red cells, and cause their destruction, chiefly in the fetal spleen. The resulting anaemia stimulates extramedullary haematopoiesis and, when severe, causes high-output cardiac failure, hepatic dysfunction, hypoalbuminaemia, and hydrops. After birth, loss of placental clearance means the newborn must conjugate the large bilirubin load from continuing haemolysis with an immature liver, producing rapidly rising unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that risks bilirubin neurotoxicity.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary red cell membrane or enzyme defects (e.g. spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency)
Cephalohaematoma or extravascular blood breakdown causing jaundice
Twin-to-twin transfusion and other causes of neonatal anaemia
additionalInvestigations: Maternal and infant blood group and antibody screening
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the newborn
Serial total and unconjugated bilirubin measurements
Full blood count with reticulocyte count and blood film
Fetal middle cerebral artery Doppler to assess for fetal anaemia antenatally
Follow-up haemoglobin to detect late anaemia
redFlags: Hydrops fetalis with severe anaemia and heart failure
Rapidly rising or very high unconjugated bilirubin threatening bilirubin encephalopathy
Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life
Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, poor feeding, hypertonia, abnormal cry)
Severe or late anaemia requiring transfusion
reference.prognosis: With antenatal surveillance, intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anaemia, and neonatal phototherapy or exchange transfusion, outcomes are generally good. Prophylactic anti-D has dramatically reduced severe Rh disease. Prognosis worsens if severe hyperbilirubinaemia progresses to kernicterus or if profound fetal anaemia and hydrops are untreated.
pitfalls: Underestimating ABO disease because it can affect a first-born and cause significant jaundice
Failing to monitor bilirubin closely and intervene before it reaches neurotoxic levels
Overlooking late anaemia in the weeks after birth once early jaundice has settled
Missing an opportunity for anti-D prophylaxis in an at-risk mother
Attributing early jaundice to physiological causes when haemolysis is occurring
